Motion No. 2
That Bill C-30 be amended in Clause 7
(a)	by striking out line 32 at page 3 and substituting the following therefor: "including the resources and lending of the International Monetary Fund and the".
(b)	by striking out line 36 at page 3 and substituting the following therefor: "goods and services and also including a detailed review of Canada's participation in the lending activities of the World Bank Group and the International Monetary Fund, with particular attention to: (a) Canada's use of its voice and vote to promote internationally recognized human rights; (b) Canadian initiatives to promote the use of loans to meet the basic human needs of the poorest and provide for a more equitable distribution of income

May 7, 1985
Bretton Woods Agreements Act in recipient countries; (c) Policy actions taken by Canada to protect the neutrality and multilateral character of the World Bank Group and International Monetary Fund and resist the excessive pursuit of rigid bilateral policies by other member nations; (d) Canadian initiatives to promote Financial adjustment policies that do not impose additional hardship on the poor."
She said: Mr. Speaker, the first subsection of this motion is primarily for clarification. Clause 7 in the present Bill is a reporting clause. It repeals the present Section 7 and substitutes the following:
7. The Minister of Finance shall, on or before the 31st day of March next following the end of each year or, if Parliament is not then sitting, on any of the first thirty days next thereafter that Parliament is sitting, submit to Parliament a report containing a general summary of operations under this Act and details of all such operations that directly affect Canada, including the resources and lending of the World Bank Group, the funds subscribed or contributed by Canada, borrowings in Canada and procurement of Canadian goods and services.
What we have done, Mr. Speaker, to make clear that this Act is also addressed to the International Monetary Fund as well as to the World Bank group, is to add the International Monetary Fund so that the latter half of the clause will read:
-and details of all such operations that directly affect Canada including the resources and lending of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank group-
There should be no difficulty with anyone supporting that clarification.
The second part of the motion is a substantive one: it tries to do something we have been trying to do in this part of the House in one fashion or another over the past many years, namely, to establish certain criteria to be followed in the lending practices of international financial institutions.
As our amendment indicates, there are four particular criteria that we have felt and continue to feel are essential in the lending practices of international financial institutions. The first of these is that particular attention should be paid to the human rights question, and that Canada's use of its voice and vote in international financial institutions should be for the purpose of promoting internationally recognized human rights. I will return to that in a moment.
The second criterion we are proposing concerns Canadian initiatives to promote the use of loans to meet the basic human needs of the poorest and to provide for more equitable distribution of income in recipient countries.
The third criterion concerns policy actions taken by Canada to protect the neutrality and multilateral character of the World Bank group and the International Monetary Fund and to resist the excessive pursuit of rigid bilateral policies by other member nations.
The final criterion we are proposing in this section for the operation of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank group is that there be Canadian initiatives to promote financial adjustment policies that do not impose additional hardship on the poor.
The way it is now in this clause, without any of the four additional criteria that I have just outlined and that are in our motion, the clause terminates with the words "procurement of
Canadian goods and services". That is the way the clause ends now. The emphasis, therefore, in the reporting process is really on what Canada only has gotten out of the operations of these international financial institutions, what procurement of Canadian goods and services. That is literally all we will get in the reporting process provided in Clause 7.
What we are saying is that there are at least four more areas about which we want to know, and we want a report to this House concerning the activities of the international financial institutions covered by this Bill. We want to know whether in the first instance human rights abuses are being taken into consideration by the World Bank group and by the International Monetary Fund before they authorize a loan.
The arguments of the officials of the Department of Finance in committee were almost contradictory. On the one hand, they said that if they included gross abuses of human rights criteria they would be "politicizing" the IMF and the World Bank. On the other hand, they pointed out that in the case of Uganda several years ago when there were gross human rights violations, it was proper that a loan should not have been extended to that country. Apparently on that occasion refusing a loan was not in fact politicizing in the case of Uganda.
We have argued time and time again that requiring international financial institutions to look at the human rights situation in a potential recipient country is in fact not a politicization. Human rights and the human rights covenant of the United Nations are universal. All countries of the world which signed the human rights covenant have effectively said that the protection of human rights is beyond politics and partisanship, that it is universal. We all said that, all of us who signed the UN covenant. Because we have all said that, we have taken it out of a narrow partisan or political realm. We have said that because we all agree on human rights and are all opposed to gross human rights abuses, we are not politicizing the issue. Indeed, as the Canadian Government has already shown when it did not support loans to Uganda, it could equally well show today that it does not support loans to countries engaging in massive abuses of human rights. We are asking for this criterion to which apparently all nations that signed the human rights covenant of the United Nations agreed. It is a criterion which is universal and is universally agreed to.
I notice, Mr. Speaker, you are indicating that my time is coming to an end. My colleagues will address this criterion further, as well as the other three criteria which we are asking to be added to give some genuine meaning to the Act and to our belief in genuine international development assistance that respects human rights and the needs of the neediest.

speakeroldname: Mr. Claude Lanthier (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I want to set the record straight and say that we, as new Members, are perfectly free to make statements, that we were not forced to do so by any Minister, that I get along perfectly well with both Ministers
May 7, 1985

and that I am free to come or not to come to the House. I offered my services this morning because my Ministers were busy, but Hon. Members may rest assured that we are perfectly free, that we are not forced in any way to defend our Government's policy, and that we take an active part in that Government. I wanted to be on the record as having said that, and now, I would like to speak more specifically to Motion No. 2.
I think the first part of the motion, namely section (a), if 1 am not mistaken, clarifies the paragraph in question.
I even think that part of the motion would be acceptable, if the motion did not include a second part that is not acceptable to us. The first part stresses, and I am not saying it is redundant to do so, that the International Monetary Fund is to be included with the World Bank. Although I think this is covered in the preambles, the amendment does provide further clarification. However, I must reiterate that we cannot accept the amendment because it is part of a more complex motion, whose second part is totally unacceptable to us.
As for the second part, it is a firm statement of intent, the substance of which we support as well, but I think it would be dangerous at this time, to make a statement of intent that might be construed by other nations as restrictive, or which might be interpreted differently in the course of time. We have seen treaties signed after the last World War which seemed to promote freedom and which proved to be a straightjacket for some nations. I think it would be better to provide a little more latitutde with respect to the principles being laid down here, so that our representatives in these institutions can exercise, not their voting rights, which are frequently made use of at the United Nations, whose proceedings I have had a chance to observe, but their powers of persuasion, since in these organizations it is more important to establish a consensus: in other words, people analyze the problems thoroughly, discuss them and instead of submitting them immediately for a vote, they use their powers of persuasion.
So, once again, as a free agent, but not reluctant to practise my English, I prepared a short speech in response to the second part of the motion.

Canada has also been a very strong supporter of efforts over the past decade to ensure that World Bank loans promote the basic human needs of the poorest people in developing countries. In part, we have supported this approach as a means of ensuring a more equitable distribution of income in recipient countries. Moreover, we have felt that this approach would help ensure that the poor would benefit regardless of the political and ethical ideologies of the particular Government which happens to be in power at the time the loan is approved. World Bank and International Development Association loans seek to address the long-term problems of the poor, and great care should be taken before turning off programs which take a long time to get started. We are confident that the World Bank is seriously pursuing the objective of improving the
Bretton Woods Agreements Act
economic lot of the poor in recipient countries and therefore deserves our strong support.
The proposed amendment would create the erroneous impression that Canada does not believe the World Bank is pursuing these objectives. The amendment talks of Canadian initiatives and policy action in these institutions. Instead, we believe the World Bank is committed and the need is for Canada to support the effective implementation and evolution, as necessary, of existing policies.
By referring to the use of Canada's vote in these institutions, the amendment also suggests a line of action which we believe could be counter-productive. Canada has sought to avoid the use of votes in the World Bank and has encouraged decisionmaking based on consensus. As a consequence, unlike the United Nations, voting is not a common practice in these institutions. Canada, by itself, could not stop a loan and if we were to encourage other countries to exercise their votes on the executive boards, we would not be able to contain the practice to our own objectives. In other words, we would likely only encourage greater politicization of these institutions.
In short, Mr. Speaker, we want to be consistent with our policy actions, as much within international organizations as within the Canadian Government itself. We would use persuasion and even change our original concept through a document or consultations paving the way for a final decision, rather than make a hasty decision such that those basic principles might eventually be harmful to us.
Keeping in mind what I have just said, I repeat that the first part of the motion is acceptable to us, because it does shed more light even though it is not exclusive since the first part of the Bill covers everything under the Bretton Woods Acts as well as the other related organizations. However, we cannot subscribe to the first part because the second part might hamper our negotiations with respect to the World Bank, the International Monetary Fund, the International Finance Corporation and the International Development Association.
Mr. Speaker, we cannot support this amendment.

Mr. Speaker, I particularly enjoyed the comments of the Hon. Member for LaSalle (Mr. Lanthier). I found it rather interesting that the Government Members in a sense support the first part of this motion, which includes the name IMF for clarification, but when it comes to the reporting of human rights, there is no way they will be on the side of that. They do not want to support the second part of the motion. They would have supported the first part, but it was part of a package. The Hon. Member for LaSalle said that the second part of the package includes not restricting Canada's behaviour to tying loans to human rights support in our development assistance, but simply the reporting of the ways and means by which we

May 7, 1985
Bretton Woods Agreements Act
were encouraging the development of human rights in those countries in which the World Bank group is associated.
I look rather incredulously across the aisle. I see the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise), the Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport (Mr. Jelinek), the Minister of State for Forestry (Mr. Merrithew) and a variety of their colleagues. Unless they speak differently, I guess I am hearing that they support the Hon. Member for LaSalle when he says that when it comes to human rights they do not want to be associated with that business, that they want to maintain the status quo.
The Hon. Member went on to read a nice statement that some bureaucrat obviously wrote, saying we should look at Canada's behaviour when it comes to human rights and at how we have ensured that all of our participation for development aid has resulted in more equality, in more egalitarian use of the aid and so on. Everyone in this House knows that the poor have become poorer and the right have become richer in almost every nation that we are presumably assisting, including Canada.
I take with some large chunks of salt some of the comments made by the Hon. Member. I do not believe he actually meant what he was saying, but was in fact reflecting the views expressed in the written statement of some bureaucrat on the government side.
I want to say a word or two about some aspects of this motion. We are asking the Government to accept this motion because it attempts to do basically three things. It attempts to ask Canada to pay some attention to human rights issues in our lending practices through the World Bank group. One could list pages and pages of countries that have received assistance from the World Bank group where respect for human rights is an absolute travesty.
I refer to countries like Chile. When Allende's elected Government was in power in Chile, the United States said that we had to stop this nonsense of supporting through the IMF and the World Bank the activities going on in Chile. As soon as that Government was replaced by General Pinochet and a totalitarian military dictatorship was imposed on the people and human rights were tossed out the window, the United States went to bat and said that now is the time for the IMF and the World Bank group to show support for the country of Chile.
We could go on with Vietnam. When Vietnam was in a state of war and there was American involvement there, the U.S. was supportive of IMF and World Bank aid. The minute they pulled out, they used their pressure to stop any assistance to South Vietnam.
In 1982 the United States Treasury identified 80 critical development issues in which the United States had sought to influence the policies of the World Bank group. That is from the United States Treasury itself. The United States said it was going to impose its heavy hand on the decision-making of that group. As a result, more and more development assistance
tended to go to those countries where human rights abuses are extremely well known.
All we are asking in this motion is that Canada pay some attention to this fact, that Canada use its influence in these world financial groups to speak out against some of these pressure tactics of the United States and support the proposals that tend to recognize the human rights abuses in a variety of countries.
The motion goes on to add one other aspect. That is that the loans to the various countries coming from the World Bank group and the IMF assist those that really need assistance. All of us know that much of that aid simply goes to perpetuate the status quo. The status quo means a country where the land is controlled by a handful of individuals. I see the Minister of Agriculture here. He knows full well that one of the difficulties that these countries face is a continuation of a monoculture type of agriculture where people are starving because they do not have land on which to grow subsistence crops. They are encouraged through their system to carry on with banana plantations, coconut plantations and so on which are designed for a handful of people and for the procurement of foreign exchange. There has to be some balance in this. Many of our assistance programs simply perpetuate the old status quo type of economies that do little, if anything, to assist the poor people in a variety of these countries.
The third part of our motion asks that Canada work to protect the multilateral character of World Bank lending. Rather than tie a lot of the assistance in some way in terms of bilateral agreements, the multilateral system should be used. Anyone who appreciates and supports the concept of economic assistance to developing our lesser developed countries will have to admit that multilateral approaches in terms of assistance are certainly better than the bilateral-tied aid situation. This motion asks that Canada use its influence so that wherever possible the multilateral approach is used. I have not read a single article or book that says that the way to go is more bilateral aid. Quite the contrary. We are just going along with what is common knowledge.
We are asking the Government to pay attention to human rights abuses in countries that receive much of the benefits of the World Bank group and the IMF. We ask that Canada pay attention to doing what it can to ensure that the people who need the support, the economic infrastructure development and the export assistance in the developing countries receive it, not simply the landed aristocracy. Or, if you like, have aid milked through a corrupt, tinpot dictatorship as the sole beneficiary of much of this particular aid. More attention should be paid by Canada to encouraging development of multilateral assistance.
I cannot imagine why anybody would vote against this motion. I hope that before we vote we will have an opportunity to hear one of the Members of the Government Party explain what is wrong with these three proposals.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few comments on Motion No. 2, particularly the second part of that motion where we are
May 7, 1985

very modestly asking that the Government give more details in its annual reports on the activities of the World Bank group and the International Monetary Fund. In particular, we list four areas where we believe the House of Commons and the Canadian public generally need to have information from our Government as to the way in which we have participated in those organizations.
As the Hon. Member for New Westminster-Coquitlam (Ms. Jewett) pointed out, we want to know how Canada has used its voice and its vote to promote internationally recognized human rights. The Parliamentary Secretary said that the Government tries to operate by consensus, but let us at least hear what our voice said when we were trying to reach consensus. Where do we stand on some of these questions?
The Task Force on the Churches and Corporate Responsibility, in its presentation to the committee last month, said that there should be the establishment of basic human rights criteria as a co-determinant for Canada's voting decisions at the IMF and the World Bank. When it talks about basic human rights, Mr. Speaker, it talks of the most narrow and restrictive meaning of that term. It was not talking about such exalted things as freedom of the press. It was talking about basic rights such as the right to be free from arbitrary arrest, detention and execution, the right to be free from torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment, and the right to be free from internal or external exile. The most basic of human rights are what we are concerned about here. We would like to see some reporting on the way in which our voice, our vote, was used in determining loans to countries such as Chile where those basic rights are not observed at present.
We want to see reporting on the way in which Canadian initiatives promote the use of loans to meet the most basic human needs of the poorest and provide for a more equitable distribution of income to recipient countries. Certainly, Hon. Members of our Party-and I would like to think Hon. Members from all Parties-would not want our aid funding to go to create a wealthy elite which is completely separated from the needs of the poorest and most needy of the people in the country to which aid is going. We do not want to create just a shiny veneer at the top of the economic heap. We want to see true development, which means working from the bottom up rather than from the top down. We want to see policy actions taken by Canada to protect the neutrality and multilateral character of the World Bank group and the IMF and to resist the excessive pursuit of rigid bilateral policies by other member nations.
It is interesting to note that when this Bill was being debated in committee, the Government said we cannot have it both ways; we cannot both be concerned about human rights and be concerned that this whole process is not going to be politicized. I would like to ask Hon. Members on the government side if they see human rights simply as a question of politics, if they see it as simply something which pertains to the particular policies of a particular government at a given
Bretton Woods Agreements Act
time, or if they see human rights and the question of politicization as something which is more basic as something quite different?
For example, we have seen the actions of the United States in the last few months in trying to block loans to Nicaragua. It is not because Nicaragua did not meet the formal criteria for the loans. In fact, the loans were approved on a technical basis. It is simply because Nicaragua does not meet some political criteria which are established by a paranoid official in the White House. We want to oppose that kind of politicization and it has nothing whatever to do, Mr. Speaker, with our insistence upon seeing that basic human rights are observed.
Finally, we want reporting on Canadian initiatives to promote financial adjustment policies which do not impose additional hardship on the poor. In the past we have seen the situation time and again where a debtor nation falls into some difficulty with the IMF with respect to its debts. The IMF goes in and establishes very rigid policies which have to be followed in order for the country to secure a rescheduling of its loan or additional credit. These policies impact most directly on the poor people in areas such as the withdrawal of food subsidies or cut-backs in social services. This is turn has led to riots, the so-called IMF riots where people have simply said: "We refuse to knuckle under to this kind of repression"; and that kind of unrest has led to further political repression and a movement away from democracy. That in turn often creates even more problems for the economy. It becomes a vicious circle.
We believe that Canada's voice should be heard in the direction of wanting to see that there are certain basic criteria which are adhered to in any IMF policy for debt rescheduling. Some of those criteria should require that debt rescheduling not result in an intolerable burden being placed upon the poorest people of the country involved.
It was interesting to note over the past week that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), when he was on his way to the summit at Bonn, said that he wanted to be a voice for the poor, for the Third World. Whether he was getting in some training because Conservative policies might soon leave Canada in a Third World, poor situation, or whether he was really concerned with speaking out on behalf of present Third World countries, I do not know, but if he is concerned about speaking out for present Third World countries, then I believe this is one area where Canada should be very active. We should make sure when we are dealing with the IMF that IMF resheduling does not impact in a way which simply adds additional burdens on the poor.
When the Task Force on the Churches and Corporate Responsibility appeared before the committee, Mr. Speaker, it pointed to three areas where it thought there should be establishment of the basic human rights criteria as a co-determinant for the granting of loans through the IMF or the World Bank. It also thought that there should be the establishment of social criteria as an integral part of the stabilization and adjustment measures negotiated between credit applicants and the IMF. When we are dealing with those countries which have been

May 7, 1985
involved with gross violations of human rights, it suggested that there could be some specific projects which would give help to those who were most poor and needy and perhaps the establishment of a basic needs criteria which would ask the question: "Does a specific project help in such areas as food, shelter, clothing or education for the people at the very lowest stratum of society?" If that is the case, perhaps we would see our way clear to make loans available in those countries, but not if the loans simply go to provide some kind of development which is going to benefit only the people at the top.
It is interesting that Section 701 of the International Financial Institutions Act of the United States has this kind of provision. The brief of the Task Force on the Churches and Corporate Responsibility states, and I quote:
Section 701 prohibits U.S. aid through multilateral institutions to "gross and consistent violators of internationally recognized human rights", unless it can be established that the aid project in question serves basic human needs. Basic human needs are defined as covering food, clothing, shelter, health and education.
This is one of the areas in which I think we should be willing to move. It is one of the areas which we want to see reported on. As my colleagues have said, we believe that this motion calling for reporting is one which should be supported on all sides of the House and I urge all Hon. Members of the Government to support it.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) for the wonderful job he did on behalf of his colleague, Frank Miller. I can understand why the Prime Minister refused to say anything in English about the election results when confronted in Bonn. The stunning victory of David Peterson and the Ontario Liberals, the Party that received the most votes of any
in Ontario, was a massive repudiation of Mulroney's seven months of broken federal promises.
The Prime Minister, on the satellite Tory love-in, said: "You can bet your mortgage on a Tory majority". As housing critic, I am calling to collect.
Today the Prime Minister blames the revenge factor on the tremendous Tory losses. Throughout this fall and winter, Members of Parliament and consumer groups have heard the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Cote) say that he intends to act on the shameful practice of tax discounting. However, yesterday the Minister reversed himself, and now he wants to consult further with a consultation paper. This paper, and yet more consultations, will take even more weeks and months. Much of the money taken comes from the federal Government's own child tax credit. Yet the Minister's reponse is more consultation. Consultation with whom, and consultation to what end? The Minister should realize that there is a point at which consultation becomes stalling, and-

Mr. Speaker, participants in the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe, designed to monitor compliance with the 1975 Helsinki Agreement signed by Canada, the United States, and 33 European countries, today commenced formal deliberations in Ottawa.
Specifically with regard to Poland, it is crucial that the participants address themselves to the human rights of the Polish people and the Solidarity movement. Lech Walesa and Father Popieluszko have become household names because they have embodied the hopes and fears of their fellow Poles who seek those fundamental rights and freedoms enjoyed by all Canadians.
Therefore it is Canada's privilege and responsibility, as a nation which takes pride in its historical role as a champion of human rights and freedoms, to support and encourage the Solidarity movement actively. This we can do by calling upon the respective Governments of Poland and the Soviet Union to uphold the terms of the Helsinki Accords with respect to Solidarity and the people of Poland.
In 1961 the late American President, John F. Kennedy, immortalized the words, "Ich bin ein Berliner", precisely because those words encapsulated his own identification with the oppressed people of East Berlin and East Germany.
Similarly today, each Canadian who values freedom and democracy, can identify with the people of Poland by proclaiming that we, too, are members of Solidarity.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I would like to continue the comments I started to make last Wednesday, which appear on page 4287 of Hansard. I mentioned the fact that in my riding, more than 15 per cent of the letters I sent were returned with the comment: "Moved: no forwarding address". However, most of the addresses were correct.
Mr. Speaker, what is the use of spending so much time and effort on communicating, if our mail does not reach its destination? Isn't every taxpayer entitled to receive prompt and equitable service from Canada Post?
As a Canadian and as the Member for Quebec East, I am very proud to serve my constituents, and I believe it would be tremendous if all Canada Post employees could feel the same pride and satisfaction with a job well done.
Mr. Speaker, the credibility of Canada Post must be restored in order to regain user confidence. Would the answer be to create another commission of enquiry?

Mr. Speaker, some of the members of Common Council of the City of Saint John have expressed their displeasure with the federal Government's tourism advertising.

In fact, the Federal Government's tourism advertising in the April issue of the magazine "Selection" emphasizes tourism in Quebec and in Southern Ontario. As for New Brunswick, the ad only mentions the Campbellton Festival and Loyalist Day.
Does the Minister not realize there are more tourist attractions in New Brunswick? Has the Government forgotten that the Canada Games will be held in that province this year? I should think that would be a very important national event.
But that is not all. The Minister of State for Tourism (Mr. McMillan) also forgot to mention in his ad the Acadian Games, the Lobster Festival, the Fisheries Festival, the Acadi-ans' National Day, and a lot more.
The people of New Brunswick have every right to be dissatisfied.

"It's very bad. It's about total neglect," said the Common Council. "The federal mandate should be larger than that." Is this what the Minister means by: "We have to back winners at the expense of losers?" Are we in New Brunswick going to be the losers?

subtopic: FIRING OF VANCOUVER SCHOOL BOARD BY PROVINCIAL GOVERNMENT
FIRING OF VANCOUVER SCHOOL BOARD BY PROVINCIAL GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) announced a Budget for May 23 and said that it would be a tough one. Yesterday the Social Credit Government of British Columbia fired the duly elected members of the Vancouver School Board because those trustees, with public support, refused to apply Draconian restraint measures, opting instead for decent education for Vancouver children.
The Vancouver trustees were elected specifically on a proeducation, anti-restraint program. Then the Government of British Columbia, in January of this year, passed a dictatorial

May 7, 1985
provision in the Education (Interim) Finance Act, which states:
On or before May 1 in each year the Board of each school district shall by by-law adopt the budget for the next fiscal year in accordance with any directives issued by the Minister.
I call upon the federal Cabinet to look closely at the disallowance power it has under Sections 56 and 90 of the Constitution Act of 1867, to strike down this anti-democratic provincial law, and to restore democracy in British Columbia. I further call upon the federal Government, which is negotiating English as a second language funding with the Government of British Columbia, to use its influence so that education dollars are spent for education.
Finally, I would draw to the attention of the Minister of Finance how restraint policies have ruined the once prosperous economy of British Columbia. In his Budget of May 23, I ask him to avoid that kind of Draconian restraint and any educational cut-backs.

subtopic: RESTORATION OF CITADEL HILL IN HALIFAX

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subtopic: RESTORATION OF CITADEL HILL IN HALIFAX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Citadel Hill in Halifax will be restored as a result of an historic agreement signed between Parks Canada and The Friends of the Citadel Society. This program is a first, and is representative of our Government's desire to have private groups take the initiative in areas where high deficits have forced government restraint.
The Friends of the Citadel have initiated a revised plan whereby the restoration, which was previously deferred, will now proceed with the co-operation of Parks Canada. This joint project, which will provide immediate employment for approximately 65 students as "period soldiers", will also see extensive portions of the Citadel's fortifications restored.
Under this momentous agreement The Friends of the Citadel have committed themselves to raising approximately $2 million over the course of the project, while Parks Canada will provide $1 million. I feel confident that the citizens of Halifax will respond with generosity and enthusiasm to this plan. I applaud the ingenuity and imagination of The Friends of the Citadel, and the sensitivity of the federal Government in implementing the restoration of Citadel Hill.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to draw the attention of this House to a crucial issue facing two major meat processing firms in New Brunswick. The future viability and existence of Hub Meat Packers Limited in Moncton, and Chippin Bros. Ltd. in Fredericton, will be in jeopardy if and when the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) signs an ERDA agreement with the Province of Prince Edward Island.
This agreement is intended to live up to a promise made by the past Liberal Government in the latter days of its mandate to provide funding to the former Canada Packers plant in Charlottetown, P.E.I. The Department of Agriculture, and the government commissioned study on the red meat industry in Altantic Canada, both cautioned against expansion of meat processing capacity in the Altantic Provinces.
The Province of P.E.I. has already expressed its intention to expand the number of hogs processed from 2,650 to 4,500 per week. Thus the activities of the federal Government, in conjunction with the Government of P.E.I., will place in jeopardy the supply of hogs and beef to the existing plants in Fredericton and Moncton.
Our Government has shown integrity in honouring past commitments, but a lack of foresight is allowing this commitment to be kept without taking precautions to protect the supply of hogs and beef to the plants in New Brunswick, or to limit the processing capacity of the P.E.I. plant. I urge the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion to co-ordinate activities with other federal government agencies to guarantee the supply of hogs and beef to New Brunswick plants so as to protect the more than 600 jobs currently in existence but in jeopardy in both Moncton and Fredericton.

subtopic: NEED TO ADOPT GLOBAL POLICY CONCERNING REFUGEES AND IMMIGRANTS IN GENERAL
NEED TO ADOPT GLOBAL POLICY CONCERNING REFUGEES AND IMMIGRANTS IN GENERAL
speechtext:
Last week, Mr. Speaker, we learned that the Progressive Conservative Government had cancelled its lease with Toronto's Avion Hotel where refugee status applicants were held. The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) stated that from now on humanitarian organizations should be responsible for sheltering and feeding a number of future refugees.
If we contrast the decisions to reduce refugee services and raise next year's immigration levels, the contradiction is even more obvious.
The Progressive Conservative Government is planning to let private organizations assume part of the refugee financial burden instead of shouldering its responsibilities and expanding refugee services at the same time as it raises immigration levels.
What we need, Mr. Speaker, is a new global policy concerning refugees and immigrants in general. This policy would cover such sectors as employment, training and social services,
May 7, 1985

as well as others more specifically related to reception and accommodation.
Therefore I urge the Progressive Conservative Government to drop its plans to let private organizations look after landed and future immigrants.

subtopic: VISIT TO NETHERLANDS BY CANADIAN VETERANS OF WORLD
VISIT TO NETHERLANDS BY CANADIAN VETERANS OF WORLD
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, yesterday, from coast to coast, Canadians must have felt pride at the hero's welcome some 2,000 Canadian veterans and veteran's spouses received from the Dutch people.

subtopic: VISIT TO NETHERLANDS BY CANADIAN VETERANS OF WORLD
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: VISIT TO NETHERLANDS BY CANADIAN VETERANS OF WORLD
speechtext:
This visit to the 40th anniversary celebration of the liberation of the Netherlands from Nazi occupation was more than a sentimental journey; it was also a message from history. For a generation Canada and the Netherlands have had a warm and secure friendship. Neither country has had aggressive desires against any other people. Each has been committed to peace. However, this anniversary of war does not contradict any of that. Rather, it reminds us that preparedness for defence is necessary for peace.
Canadians died in the Netherlands in 1944 and 1945 because the democracies were not prepared to resist Nazi aggression in 1939 and 1940. Our desire for peace in the 1980s must benefit from this hard lesson. Sir Winston Churchill said another name for World War II could have been the "unnecessary war", unnecessary because it could have been prevented. This anniversary of World War II reminds us that if Canadians are never to return to Europe and war again, Canada and its allies must be prepared to prevent aggression by being prepared to resist it.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. The unfortunate failure of the Bonn Summit to move forward the agenda on world trade threatens to accelerate protectionist sentiment in the U.S. Congress and, indeed, in the European Economic Community, potentially leaving Canada in a very vulnerable position.
The Prime Minister will understand that any new trade barriers in the U.S. would be of grave concern to Canada. My question relates to his answer yesterday in the House when he told Members that he could not guarantee that Canada would receive any exemption from American trade barriers, yet a number of weeks ago in Quebec City he signed a joint declaration with the President of the U.S. moving both Canadians and Americans toward freer trade. Would the Prime Minister be good enough to explain to the House just what kind of arrangement he has with the President of the U.S.?

It is interesting, Mr. Speaker, after listening to the Liberal Party castigate the Government for trying to develop closer and sounder commercial relations with the U.S., to find all of a sudden the Grits are getting worried. Well they should be, because there are three million Canadian jobs which depend on developing the kind of mature and responsible relationships we have tried to rebuild since the election campaign, and with which, I am sure it is widely known, my right hon. friend is in general agreement. Indeed, there was a failure to reach unanimity at Bonn, but Canada, along with other countries, worked very strenuously to preserve the multilateral trading process and the thrust toward liberalization of trade. The Quebec meeting was all the more important because there was a declaration of intention there between the U.S. and Canada.
We hope there will not be a breakdown in multilateral moves toward trade liberalization but, if there is, we believe that the efforts we have initiated will stand us in good stead in consideration of options vis-a-vis the U.S., all of which will be designed to protect Canadian jobs vis-a-vis the U.S. market.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my criticism of the Prime Minister's position at the Quebec Summit was that he over-estimated the President's clout with the U.S. Congress, which is where our problem is going to lie.

However, besides our concern over American trade barriers, Canadians are also worried about interest rates. When in Bonn, the Prime Minister should have raised the interest rates

issue with President Reagan. How come he did not manage to convince his friend the President to include in the final communique a plan of action to lower world interest rates?

Mr. Speaker, we did discuss at length the problems created by interest rates and their impact on future economic recovery. Should one care to read the communique, one would indeed note direct references to the causes of our interest rates. It must be said, one is the extraordinary indebtedness which our relatively small population has inherited from the previous Government. When the other nations were in a position to appreciate the full extent of the debt which Canada inherited from the Liberals, they were quite horrified by such indebtedness. That is why our economic recovery program is much more serious and much more appropriately geared to the private sector.
On several occasions, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance had explained that interest rates are linked with the American monetary policy.

subsubtopic: GREAT LAKES POLLUTION-CUT IN UNITED STATES PROGRAM FUNDING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my final supplementary question arises out of our relationship with the U.S. I was disturbed, as were I believe many Members, to learn of the recent decision of the U.S. Senate Committee on the environment which effectively cut about $175 million from pollution programs in states bordering the Great Lakes. subsubtopic: GREAT LAKES POLLUTION-CUT IN UNITED STATES PROGRAM FUNDING

subtopic: TRADE WITH NICARAGUA-POSITION OF UNITED STATES GOVERNMENT
TRADE WITH NICARAGUA-POSITION OF UNITED STATES GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Right Hon. Prime Minister. In the light of the decision made yesterday by the U.S. Treasury Department to monitor closely Canadian branches of U.S. companies that trade with Nicaragua, could the Prime Minister give Canadian businessmen the assurance that they can continue to trade with that country, without fear of reprisals? Furthermore, could we perhaps ask companies, even the branches of U.S. companies, to sell agricultural equipment and medical supplies, which are both extremely important to the economic survival of the people of Nicaragua, without incurring any punitive action on the part of the American Government?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: TRADE WITH NICARAGUA-POSITION OF UNITED STATES GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have made it clear since the American policy was announced that it is their policy and not ours. We have sought and received assurances that American sanctions will not affect Canadian exports, including those in the sensitive fields which the Hon. Member has mentioned.
The Member refers to reports out of the United States that Americans will be closely monitoring Canadian activity. If that is the case, I can say that there will be a whole lot of monitoring going on, because we intend to monitor extremely closely both the formulation and application of any regulations that the Americans might bring in with regard to their sanctions to ensure that they do not limit, in any way at all, Canadian exports to, or Canadian relations with, Nicaragua.

Member will ensure that Members of his Party do not say that, because we want to help the poor people of Nicaragua; Canadians do not want to persecute them.

Government, and I would hope the interest of Parliament, is that the Government of Canada and the Parliament of Canada can act, during the period when these sanctions are in place, in every way possible to encourage econmic strength and political stability in Latin America. subtopic: REQUEST THAT EXPORT CREDITS BE EXTENDED TO NICARAGUA
REQUEST THAT EXPORT CREDITS BE EXTENDED TO NICARAGUA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is also directed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs and follows up on the very good statement he has just made. Is Canada now prepared to extend export credits to Nicaragua and to Canadian firms that are willing and able to undertake increased exports of fertilizers, pesticides, machine parts, and so on? Will he now say yes to extended export credits to both Nicaragua and those firms?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REQUEST THAT EXPORT CREDITS BE EXTENDED TO NICARAGUA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at this time in the afternoon of this particular Tuesday I am not prepared to say yes to the question that has just been raised by the Hon. Member. We are going to look at the policies that are brought in by the United States. We are going to look particularly to ensure that there is no extra-territorial application. We will then make judgments as to anything else that Canada should do.
I have already made it very clear that the Government of Canada does not intend to have its policies changed by the American introduction of sanctions. We do not intend to change the aid and development program we have put in place. We do not intend to change the plans of the Minister for External Relations to visit Central America and Nicaragua later this summer. We do not intend to change our strong and unequivocal support for the Contadora process.

Mr. Speaker, will we do something to fill the enormous gap that is going to be caused by the U.S. embargo? The one big thing we could do is to extend export credits.
The Minister for External Relations will not be going for several weeks. Since we have no mission in Nicaragua, will the Minister consider sending a special envoy now from his Department to Nicaragua to determine the economic and other needs of the Nicaragua people and ways in which Canada might further the excellent work we are already doing? The envoy could report back to the Minister on the additional things we could do to be helpful.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the acknowledgement of the Hon. Member that the work being done by the Government of Canada in Nicaragua is excellent. Indeed, I would go further than that and say that the interest that has been shown
Oral Questions
by private Canadian groups and individuals has also been excellent.
I want to know what is happening in Nicaragua as a result of the sanctions that have been announced. If special means are required to find new information on what is happening there, we will certainly do that. First, I want to see the exact nature of the sanctions that are being imposed. I want a specific idea of what is at issue here. Then we can begin to see if it is useful for Canada to add to the development work we are involved in for the support of Cantadora and the other very extensive support we have already given to the process of stability and peace in Central America.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. Yesterday I asked why the subject of interest rates had not figured prominently at the Boon Summit and why the Prime Minister did not ask President Reagan to agree to a world monetary conference. The Minister of Finance responded that Finance Ministers discussed the importance of lowering interest rates. Did the Prime Minister then voice this concern to President Reagan and stress to him the need for a world conference on reform of the international monetary system, which is what France was advocating?

Mr. Speaker, that was responded to by the Minister of Finance yesterday. France put forth its views in regard to a monetary conference. Those views were not shared by its European partners in the Economic Community, nor were they vigorously shared by other participants.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance has previously said publicly at the IMF meetings that there is a need for the industrialized countries to work in concert to reduce their interest rates. It seems as though the Minister of Finance may take whatever position he wishes with his counterparts, but cannot count on the Prime Minister to back him up if those positions in any way appear to threaten our so-called special relationship with the U.S.
What exactly was the situation? Did the Prime Minister try, without success, to influence President Reagan, or did he simply side with President Reagan, as President Mitterand indicated, in an effort to protect that special relationship?

Mr. Speaker, perhaps I can clarify some misunderstanding which the Hon. Member clearly has on this topic. Frence wants a major Bretton Woods type of conference. Those are the words of President Mitterand. We and other members of the summit

May 7, 1985
Oral Questions
nations have said that we do not need a major Bretton Woods type of conference. However, it would be helpful to take the report of the Group of Ten Finance Ministers that will be tabled in Tokyo in June and study it further in Seoul at the IMF meeting and possibly come up with some evolutionary changes in the system, but not a revolutionary change like a major Bretton Woods type conference for which President Mitterrand seems to be asking.

Maybe you want to get a better gumshoe; I don't know.
I can tell the Hon. Member that it is true that we obviously receive from time to time reports of commissions of inquiry and other recommendations. In this particular case the Deputy Prime Minister undertook a long overdue review of all existing ongoing programs to ensure the effective use of taxpayers' dollars. I have no recollection of that specific matter, but 1 can assure him that that would not have been our intent, in any case.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. On April 19 he said that for the coming fiscal year there would be no program cuts affecting native people's programs. Will he confirm that, on or about the same day, Cabinet considered a document that was submitted by the Deputy Prime Minister and supported by 11 other Departments, that contained recommendations for budget cuts in native people's programs for the fiscal years 1986-87 and 1987-88 in the sums of $133.9 million and $178.4 million respectively?

Mr. Speaker, the President of the Treasury Board signals his unawareness of that specific document. While I would have to refresh my memory, I have no recollection of that particular matter.
What has happend from time to time is that the Deputy Prime Minister reviews with groups from the outside, the private sector, labour unions and others, all of the programs as they exist in the Government of Canada, to try to save the taxpayers money and deliver services more efficiently to the people of Canada. In the course of that review we have received reports from time to time, and any definitive action thereon will of course come in budgetary statements, or otherwise.

Mr. Speaker, it is written in the document in question, which was prepared by the Deputy Prime Minister, that it has the support of 11 Ministers of the Crown and is submitted for Cabinet consideration. It also contains a media strategy that is intended to convey or generate a certain impression of effects on the native people of Canada, after the Budget comes down.
In light of this, and the fact that the document recommends many changes in programs affecting native people and cuts out millions of dollars from the programs, does it not make a mockery of the Prime Minister's commitment to consultation, when the leading native people's groups have not been consulted at all about this outrageous proposal?

A point of order, Mr. Speaker. May I respectfully make a comment on the point you raised earlier and about which you just spoke? I have reviewed Beauchesne's and I do not find anything in the Fifth Edition, the latest edition, saying that the preferred or priority method of dealing with petitions is to table them and that it is only by exception that they should be read out. Citation 692 of Beauchesne's Fifth Edition says:
While a Member may, if he desires, present a petition from his place in the House during Routine Proceedings and before the Introduction of Bills, he may also present his petition by filing it with the Clerk of the House.
So I submit with the utmost respect that it is only by way of exception that a Member may present petitions to the House by filing them with the Clerk, and that the principal method is by reading them out. While there may be a citation which, on the surface, suggests the opposite, that citation is in the Fourth Edition, and I respectfully submit that it has been replaced by the citation 1 read out from the Fifth Edition.
Therefore, I respectfully submit that so long as the Hon. Member does not make a speech or present any argument in support of the petition, there is nothing to prevent him or her, if they so wish, from presenting any number of petitions from his or her place in the House rather than simply filing them.

I respect the argument of the Hon. Member but I suggest that there is something, and that is the ruling of Mr. Speaker Francis in June of 1984. I misquoted the date earlier but this matter has been dealt with and I invite the Hon. House Leader to refer to page 4587 and page 4588 of Hansard of June 12, 1984, when the matter arose. The Hon. Member is quite correct, it is Beauchesne's Fourth Edition, Citation 339, which says differently, and I think it is because of the differences between the Fourth and Fifth Editions of Beauchesne's that we have developed our own practice about how long a Member is allowed to continue presenting the same petition verbally before the Speaker interrupts.

speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should take the necessary steps to ensure, that the Chief Electoral Officer, in future elections, make all polling stations in urban areas easily accessible to the elderly and the handicapped.
He said: Mr. Speaker, as you have noticed during the past two hours, our Party is concerned with the elderly and those members of society who need help. We are concerned with people who are in need of social security and who look to the Government for stability and security of income when they reach a certain age at which they want to be able to rely on some form of stable pension income, regardless of their social and marital status. What has happened in the last two hours is an example of the commitment that our Party has to that general principle.
Our record is long and substantial. Inspired by these basic principles, I put forward this motion today. It says, in essence, that the Chief Electoral Officer ought to ensure that in every federal election the polling stations in urban areas, or for that matter in any part of the country, be easily accessible to the elderly and the handicapped.
There are very good reasons for putting this motion to you, Mr. Speaker. In recent elections, and particularly the last one, there has been an increasingly frequent practice of using buildings that are not easily accessible to the elderly and the handicapped because they have long stairways or corridors. Some of these buildings can only be approached by a series of steps and corridors which make it difficult for people of a certain age or with a physical handicap.
I refer in particular to certain large school buildings in which polling stations may be located in the basement or on the second floor. I refer in particular to other institutional buildings where accessibility leaves much to be desired. I make the point that the instructions must be clear and vigorous. The Chief Electoral Officer of Canada must play a leadership role. His instructions to the returning officers in each riding must be very clear and to the effect that the selection of polling stations must take into account the basic principle included in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms that the elderly and the handicapped must be given consideration in the arrangements which lead to the electoral process.
The Disabled and the Handicapped
On more than one occasion in the last election 1 was virtually reproached by a few electors who pointed out to me, with a certain degree of unhappiness, if not indignation, the fact that they would not be able to get into the building because of lack of access for wheelchairs. They would not be able to reach the polling station inside the large institution because they could not climb the stairs. Unfortunately and regrettably, some people simply give up their right to vote because of these considerations.
At a time when the whole thrust of our society is directed at understanding, recognizing and facilitating the participation of the elderly and the handicapped in public life, this matter requires close consideration by the Chief Electoral Officer. On many occasions, instead of utilizing large institutions, it would be better to adopt the old practice of using private homes. There is usually a side entrance and very few steps. The whole approach is much less cumbersome, particularly since a car can be parked in a driveway or very close to the entrance. I am not saying that this is the only solution, but I submit that an approach which takes into account the requirements of the elderly and the handicapped is most desirable.
In raising this motion, I urge the Chief Electoral Officer to take note of the experience that we had in Davenport in the last election. I am sure that a number of other Members have had the same experience on occasion. The numbers are not large, but that is not the principle at stake. It is an important principle which recognizes that the elderly and the handicapped must be given easy access to the voting process. That is what is at stake here and that is the reason for the motion.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would like to add a comment on the plight of unlisted electors, a matter which is not necessarily included in my motion. I am glad to see that it is recognized in the Private Members' motion of my colleague. I refer to individuals who discover on election day that they are not able to vote because their names are not on the voters' list.
Over the years we have developed an interesting, competent, and capable technique for resolving this problem in the rural voting areas of Canada. According to the Act, in those areas you can still be placed on the voters' list on the day preceding election day. That has been resolved to the satisfaction of many voters who, in the past, were dissatisfied and very disappointed when they discovered they were not on the list. However, this problem has not yet been resolved in urban Canada. Some people do not know that before every election a new enumeration is made and a new list prepared. Unless on elector is aware of the deadlines and procedures, there is potential for an elector to be omitted. He will continue to be omitted in future elections. That happens all the time in our society.
As a result of technological advancement and the equipment that is made available as a result of the chip, surely there must be a solution for urban voters who discover the day before an election that they have been omitted from the list they may be

It is essential that people who care to vote and discover their absence from a given list the day before an election be allowed to vote, if they qualify, by way of a last minute registration.

subsubtopic: ADVISABILITY OF ENSURING EASY ACCESS TO POLLING STATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to talk to this motion put forward by the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia). He should be congratulated for giving us the opportunity to do so.
The motion reads:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should take the necessary steps to ensure, that the Chief Electoral Officer, in future elections, make all polling stations in urban areas easily accessible to the elderly and the handicapped.
I would go further than what is called for in the motion because, as some Members know, I was a member of the Special Committee on the Disabled and the Handicapped which essentially made the same recommendation in 1981.
It is also referred to by the Chief Electoral Officer of Canada in a 1984 statutory report. His recommendation concerning the motion we are debating today can be found on page 47 of that report. He said that Section 33(1) of the Act which defines some of the physical requirements of a polling station should be modified to comply with recommendations made by the Special Committee on the Disabled and the Handicapped. He goes on to recommend that subsection 33(1) be amended to state that polling stations should be established in premises of convenient access which, as far as possible, shall provide level access.
I am not at all convinced that it would require an amendment to the Canada Elections Act in order to make a polling station accessible to disabled, handicapped or aged persons. It would seem to me that all that would be required is the
political will to allow all eligible Canadians to exercise their democratic right to vote in a federal election campaign.
The Chief Electoral Officer appeared before the Special Committee on the Disabled and the Handicapped and made a submission. He further sent representatives to appear before the committee at a public hearing. While these submissions did not indicate that there were any problems of accessibility for disabled voters, the subsequent testimony from witnesses at the hearing clearly revealed that such problems do indeed exist.
In Manitoba, the Elections Act has been amended to help provide accessibility to disabled voters. In the first instance, the returning officer is instructed to locate polling stations in permises to which the voters have access from the street without going up or down stairs.
The Manitoba Elections Act also states that in the case of a disabled person who cannot enter the existing polling place without difficulty, the returning officer should remove the ballot box, along with all ballots and documents in the polling place, and take it to a place in close proximity where it is accessible to the person, such as an automobile outside the polling station.
The special committee cites this Manitoba experience as a possible model for federal legislation. In the meantime, I believe the issue could be further debated before the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections. I know that the statutory report of the Chief Electoral Officer is before that committee and I know that whether or not the House chooses to refer this subject to another committee or to kill it by talking it out, the subject matter will still be discussed before that committee. Therefore, it will not disappear or go away. It would be much more preferable if the House were to deal with it in a forthright and honest way today rather than simply to talk it out as Governments usually are wont to do.
Throughout the hearings of the special committee, it heard complaints that the voting system throughout Canada makes it difficult for many disabled Canadians to travel to polls on election day. The one exception to these complaints was the Province of Manitoba which has made provisions for a postal vote system for provincial elections.
Under the Manitoba Elections Act, the returning officer receives an application by mail at least ten days before the polling day, and returns an initial ballot to the voter at least seven days before the polling day. This ballot is then marked and sealed in a plain envelope, which is placed into another special envelope which is printed in the form of a certificate.
On the certificate envelope, two people must be identified: the voter, plus another person who is authorized to vote in the same electoral division. The second person must certify that the first person's information is correct. The voter can then send the ballot and the certificate to the Chief Electoral Officer by any means before the closing of the polls. In the case of postal disruptions, the ballots may be picked up by the division returning officer, or be dropped off by friends or family.
May 7, 1985

In the last Manitoba provincial election, 900 mail-in votes were received and were mostly from urban voters. Manitoba's Chief Electoral Officer advertised the details of the postal vote and felt that the subsequent results were satisfactory.
The present policy of centralizing polling places serves the needs of the office of the Chief Electoral Officer, but it ignores many of the needs of the voting public, especially of those Canadian citizens who are disabled. Centralization makes it easier for electoral officers to organize the vote count, but it makes it more difficult for many voters to reach the voting place. Centralization again may cut the costs of the office of the Chief Electoral Officer of running a national electoral organization, but at the price of depriving many Canadians of their votes. It is totally contradictory for the federal Government to espouse a policy of maximum voter participation on the one hand, and a policy of restricted access to polling places on the other. This centralized policy, in my view, should have been ended years ago when this committee made that recommendation. It is certainly not too late for this House to instruct the Chief Electoral Officer to do it now before the next election comes.
Many of the problems the disabled voters encounter at polling stations can be solved by educating the people responsible for those facilities. This includes deputy returning officers and their staffs. If these individuals become familiar with the needs of the disabled voter at the very outset of an election period, the many potential conflicts and problems of accessibility could be eliminated. Since the polling station personnel must go through an orientation session as a requirement of their job, this additional information regarding disabled voters will entail very little extra cost in time.
As I said at the outset, I am not convinced at all that it would take an amendment to the Canada Elections Act in order to provide disabled individuals with the full right to exercise their vote. Simple political will to make sure it happens could make it so. There are some physical difficulties in some electoral ridings, I suppose, with electoral returning officers continually going back to the same places that they found to be suitable in the past, such as old church buildings, schools, and that kind of thing. Simply because it has been good enough for those returning officers in the past does not mean to say that it is good enough for the person who is trying to exercise his vote, such as disabled elderly Canadians.
There is another issue that I want to touch on, one that does not deal specifically with accessibility at the polling stations, that is, the accessibility of individuals who are confined to psychiatric institutions and simply because of that they are denied the right to vote. By the way, Mr. Speaker, the Province of Ontario finally smartened up last year and amended its Elections Act to allow individuals who are confined in psychiatric institutions to exercise their right to vote, and to recognize that simply because an individual may be mentally disabled at some point in his or her life does not mean to say that that person cannot exercise good judgment in casting a
The Disabled and the Handicapped
ballot in an election campaign. It also displays a certain kind of mental attitude toward individuals who are mentally disabled or who are temporarily mentally disabled. The results of two elections in Ontario, the series of by-elections last fall, when amendments to that legislation were in effect, and the recent election of last Thursday proved that there were no difficulties or problems created by those amendments at all. The effect of these amendments was very much appreciated by many of those individuals in those institutions because it helped them to recognize in the period of recovery that they were treated as able-bodied citizens and treated with some respect for their illness.
The Canadian Mental Health Association and other organizations appeared before the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections about three or four weeks ago and made a very strong case for an amendment under the Canada Elections Act which would remove that blatant discrimination against people who are mentally disabled or mentally handicapped. We are not talking about the criminally insane. We are talking about people who suffer a mental disability, and if anyone has taken a look at the studies over the last several years about the effects of high unemployment in this country, the effects of the tremendous social pressures placed on people, they will realize that any one of us could suffer a mental disorder at any time.
It seems to me that in that light politicians, and especially the ones here for this debate, should act in a responsible way. They should not talk out this motion. Even though I do support the motion itself, I do not feel it goes far enough in addressing the problem. At the very least if it were referred to a committee, as the Hon. Member for Davenport suggests and requests, the matter could be fully aired and debated. Witnesses could be heard and they could make their own case in a much more substantive way than we possibly can here.
